text.p: EntreMed Inc said Tuesday an expansion of the number of brain cancer patients currently under observation in the National Cancer Institute- sponsored Phase II clinical trials using thalidomide treatment.

The collaborative clinical trials agreement, established in 1995 between the two organizations and Bristol-Myers Squibb Co, was designed to study the anticancer effects of thalidomide in breast, prostate and brain cancer as well as Kaposi's sarcoma.

The brain cancer trials began in March 1996 with the intent to treat 15 progressive glioblastoma multiformae patients. Based on preliminary results to date, the enrollment was increased to 35 patients in October, EntreMed said.

The decision to increase the number of patients was made in part by assessing results of Magnetic Resonance Imaging scans after finding a suggestion of reduction in tumor size in two of the 15 initial patients. Adverse neurological events, which could be attributed to either the progression of brain tumor growth or effects of the drug, have also been observed, it said.

In preclinical animal studies, thalidomide was shown to inhibit new blood vessel growth. The growth of new blood vessels, or angiogenesis, plays a critical role in cancer, blindness and arthritis, the company explained.

In 1994, Drs. Robert D'Amato and M. Judah Folkman of Children's Hospital in Boston discovered the antiangiogenic properties of thalidomide. They demonstrated that thalidomide could prevent the formation of new blood vessels and starve tumors, suggesting it may block cancer growth in humans.

EntreMed chief executive John W. Holaday commented, "We are pleased to learn of the preliminary findings suggestive of positive results and the decision to expand these clinical trials. At present, there is no established therapeutic treatment for glioblastoma multiformae."
